structure.title: Fitts I–XIII · A hall nobody can sleep in
structure.text: The poem first gives the Danes a royal ancestry and a magnificent building. Grendel's nightly visits make the hall uninhabitable. A young Geat arrives to take on the job Hrothgar's own men have been unable to do.

structure.title: Fitts XIV–XXXI · The price of a victory
structure.text: Songs, gifts and speeches turn the encounter into public memory. Grendel has a mother, however, and the hall has offered her a reason for retaliation that its human occupants ought to find familiar.

structure.title: Fitts XXXII–XLIII · A king faces a dragon
structure.text: Years pass. Beowulf now has a people to protect and a hoard nearby has been disturbed. Undertaking danger on his own means something quite different for an ageing king than it did for an adventurous visitor.

people.name: Hrothgar
people.text: His hall was designed for giving treasure, sharing food and hearing songs. Its desolation measures a political failure as well as a physical danger. He has experience to offer a younger hero about what lasts.

people.name: Wiglaf
people.role: A young man in Beowulf's following
people.text: He remembers what gifts commit a warrior to do. When that commitment becomes expensive, remembering it can separate a companion from the men who once sat beside him at dinner.

people.name: Beowulf
people.role: A visitor who volunteers for a watch
people.text: His offer to take a night in the Danish hall is also a public account of who he thinks he is. The people at the feast have to decide what weight his account deserves. As his own position changes, the question of whose lives he is entitled to risk changes with it.

context.title: Treasure in circulation
context.text: A ring given publicly binds giver and receiver in mutual obligation. A heap of gold shut in the ground does something very different. The poem has good reason to describe both kinds of treasure so carefully.

notice.text: Listen to stories told during celebrations.
notice.why: Kin-slaying, failed alliances and approaching wars get into the songs. The people at the feast can celebrate a victory while knowing how little it guarantees their children.

notice.text: Whose loss will start another fight?
notice.why: Grief need not end with burial. Throughout the poem somebody survives with a grievance, and decisions about whose grievance counts are rarely disinterested.

opening: A king builds a hall where his people can feast, hear songs, and feel secure together. Every night a creature comes to tear that security apart. Beowulf arrives from across the sea offering to fight it without a sword, staking his name on a promise nobody else can fulfil. The poem has the direct excitement of a monster story, surrounded by a darker knowledge: halls burn, loyalties fail, and a people cannot build a lasting future solely on the strength of one extraordinary man.
